tool.name: SlopePositionClassification
tool.summary: Classifies a DEM into slope-position classes (valley, lower / middle / upper slope, flat, ridge) from a Topographic Position Index (TPI) plus slope, using a saved classification system. The TPI and slope are computed internally from the DEM (no Spatial Analyst extension), or you may supply pre-computed rasters.
tool.usage:
The Topographic Position Index (TPI; Weiss 2001, after Guisan et al. 1999) is simply the difference between a cell's elevation and the average elevation of a neighborhood around it: positive where a cell sits above its surroundings (hills, ridges), negative where it sits below them (valleys, channels), near zero on flats and on mid-slopes. Slope Position classification turns TPI (plus slope, to tell flats from mid-slopes) into named classes such as valley bottom, lower slope, mid-slope, upper slope, and ridge.
Neighborhood size is the scale of the analysis, and it matters as much as any other choice. TPI is inherently scale-dependent: the same point can be a valley bottom at one scale and a hilltop at another, and both are valid. A small neighborhood captures small, local hills and hollows; a large neighborhood captures broad ridges and valleys. Choose the scale that matters for your question -- a wide-ranging animal such as a cougar responds to major ridgelines hundreds of feet high, not to minor bumps underfoot, so you would use a larger neighborhood. Radius may be given in cells or in ground units (meters, feet, ...); a circular neighborhood uses all cells within the radius, while an annulus (a ring set by an inner and outer radius) considers only cells in a distance band. Because the neighborhoods here are computed exactly, they avoid the cell-rounding quirks of some focal-statistics implementations.
Raw versus standardized TPI -- primarily a property of the classification system, and when computing on-the-fly also the TPI-type dropdown on this dialog (which defaults to what the system expects). Raw TPI is in the DEM's elevation units, so a threshold is absolute: a 100 m hill is read the same way everywhere. This is usually the more appropriate choice for ecological and wildlife questions, where absolute relief is what an organism experiences (Dickson and Beier used raw TPI thresholds in their cougar-movement study). Standardized TPI expresses the value relative to the variability of TPI (whole raster, or the local neighborhood in the SD units), so a cell's class depends on how variable its surroundings are -- a 1 m bump on a plain and a 100 m hill in the mountains can fall in the same class. Standardized units (Weiss's own default) are useful when you want a classification that adapts to each landscape or is comparable across very different terrains, but they can be ecologically misleading. The classification systems store which units each threshold uses; edit them in the Classification System Builder.
Classification systems are reusable, named rule sets (the class thresholds, names, and colors) saved as JSON in a per-user location that survives add-in reinstalls. This tool lists the slope-position systems it finds there; the bundled defaults are Weiss's 6-class, Dickson and Beier's 4-class, and the Corridor Designer 4-Class Topographic Position system -- the corridor-analysis classification from the CorridorDesigner tutorial (canyon bottom / flat-gentle slope / steep slope / ridgetop, raw TPI with +/-12 m thresholds and a 6-degree slope split; compute the TPI with a 200 m circular radius on a meters DEM to reproduce the tutorial exactly). Create or edit systems -- including per-class colors, which symbolize the output when it is added to the map -- with the Classification System Builder. Classification is applied cell-by-cell in one pass (a class is the AND of its criteria; where classes overlap, the lowest class value wins); no Esri Con or Spatial Analyst is used.
References: Weiss, A. 2001. Topographic Position and Landforms Analysis. ESRI International User Conference poster. Guisan, A., S. B. Weiss, and A. D. Weiss. 1999. GLM versus CCA spatial modeling of plant species distribution. Plant Ecology 143:107-122 (https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1009841519580). Jenness, J. 2006. Topographic Position Index (tpi_jen.avx) extension for ArcView 3.x (http://www.jennessent.com/arcview/tpi.htm).

dialogReference.para: Choose how the tool obtains the TPI and slope it classifies:

Calculate TPI and Slope on-the-fly from DEM (default) -- the tool computes both from an input DEM using the neighborhood, TPI-type, and slope settings below. Only the "Calculate on-the-fly (from DEM)" parameters apply.

Use Existing TPI and Slope Rasters -- the tool classifies TPI and slope rasters you already have (for example, outputs of the Topographic Position Index tool). Only the "Use existing rasters" parameters apply; the DEM is not needed.

The tool classifies whatever TPI and slope values it is given as-is -- it does not re-derive raw, standardized, or percentile forms. The classification system's units are used only to warn about a possible mismatch; the tool always still runs.

The elevation raster (DEM), single band -- required when the source is "Calculate TPI and Slope on-the-fly from DEM"; ignored (and greyed out) when using existing rasters. Projected and geographic (latitude/longitude) coordinate systems are both supported; on a geographic DEM distances are handled per row on the spheroid, so a ground-unit radius changes with Latitude in order to maintain a true circle on the ground.

The saved slope-position classification system to apply (the class thresholds, names, and colors). The list is read from the per-user store; the bundled defaults are the Weiss 6-class, Dickson and Beier 4-class, and Corridor Designer 4-Class Topographic Position systems. Author new systems with the Classification System Builder. When you pick a system, the on-the-fly TPI-type and slope-units dropdowns default to what the system expects, though you may override them.

The output integer class raster, carrying a Value / Class_Name attribute table and a color map from the classification system (including any per-class opacity, so e.g. a hillshade can show through selected classes) so it draws as named, colored classes. Cells matching no class (or outside the data) are unclassified. Any unit-compatibility warnings are also written to the output's metadata. A name is suggested from the input.
Circle (all cells within the radius) or Annulus (a ring between an inner and outer radius). On-the-fly only.

The (outer) neighborhood radius, in the units chosen below. This sets the Spatial Scale (aka Bandwidth), of the analysis -- larger radii capture broader landforms. See the tool help for how to choose it. On-the-fly only.
For an annulus, the inner radius of the ring (cells nearer than this are excluded). Ignored for a circle. On-the-fly only.
Cells or a ground unit (Meters, Kilometers, Feet, Miles). A ground-unit radius is converted to a number of cells using the DEM's cell size. On-the-fly only.

On a geographic (latitude/longitude) DEM the cell size in meters is worked out separately for the east-west (width) and north-south (height) directions -- the east-west width is computed per row on the spheroid and shrinks toward the poles, while the north-south height is essentially constant -- and the radius is converted to a cell count on each axis independently. This produces an elliptical kernel in pixel space that is a true circle on the ground; and because the east-west width changes with Latitude, the horizontal radius (in cells) is recomputed row by row, so the neighborhood stays a true circle on the ground at every latitude.
Which form of TPI to compute from the DEM, when calculating on-the-fly:
Raw (elevation units) -- elevation minus neighborhood mean, in the DEM's vertical units (absolute relief; usually best for ecological questions).
Neighborhood standard deviation -- the raw TPI divided by the neighborhood standard deviation of elevation (Weiss's standardized form).
Percentile -- the percentage of neighborhood cells lower than the focal cell.

This defaults to the form the selected classification system expects, but you may change it. If it does not match the system's units the tool warns and still runs. (The whole-raster DEM-scale standardized form is intentionally not offered here, because it tracks absolute elevation rather than neighborhood position.)
The DEM's elevation units (Meters or Feet), used for the slope calculation. Detected and locked when the DEM defines a vertical coordinate system; you choose only when it does not. On-the-fly only.

Planar (default) or Geodesic slope for a projected DEM; geographic DEMs are always geodesic. Planar matches Esri's Slope tool; Geodesic corrects projection scale distortion and matters mainly for large-extent or highly distorted projections. On-the-fly only.

Compute slope in Degrees or Percent rise, when calculating on-the-fly. This defaults to the units the selected classification system's slope thresholds assume; if you choose the other units the tool warns (its slope thresholds may not apply) and still runs. The chosen units are stamped into any saved slope raster. On-the-fly only.

Optional. When calculating on-the-fly, save the generated TPI raster to this path (stamped with its TPI type). Leave blank to keep it in memory only -- it is an intermediate and is never written. On-the-fly only.
Optional. When calculating on-the-fly, save the generated slope raster to this path (stamped with its slope units). Leave blank to keep it in memory only. On-the-fly only.

The pre-computed TPI raster to classify, when the source is "Use Existing TPI and Slope Rasters". It must match the slope raster's extent and cell size. Its values are classified as-is. If it was made by the Topographic Position Index tool, its TPI type is read from its metadata for the compatibility warning; otherwise declare it below.
The pre-computed slope raster to classify, when using existing rasters. It must match the TPI raster's extent and cell size. Required when the classification system uses slope.

Optional. Declare what kind of TPI the existing raster holds (Raw, Neighborhood standard deviation, DEM-scale standard deviation, or Percentile) when it is not stamped in the raster's metadata. This is used only to warn about possibly incompatible units; the tool still runs even if a warning is shown. Leave blank if you do not want to declare it.

Optional. Declare the units (Degrees or Percent) of the existing slope raster when they are not stamped in its metadata. Used only to warn about possibly incompatible units; the tool still runs even if a warning is shown. Leave blank if you do not want to declare it.

scriptExample.title: Slope Position example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Weiss 6-class from a DEM (300 m circular neighborhood), then a second run classifying existing TPI and slope rasters. The comment block lists every valid choice for the list-driven parameters; pass these strings exactly as shown. The classification systems listed are the bundled defaults -- any system you have created or edited in the Classification System Builder is equally valid (pass its name as shown in the Builder).
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
# ---- valid options for the list-driven parameters ------------------------ # tpi_source: "Calculate TPI and Slope on-the-fly from DEM" # "Use Existing TPI and Slope Rasters" # system (bundled; user-created systems from the Classification System # Builder are also valid -- this list is not exhaustive): # "Weiss 6-Class Slope Position" # "Weiss 6-Class Slope Position, using Raw TPI values" # "Weiss 6-Class Slope Position, using Percentile TPI values" # "Dickson & Beier 4-Class Slope Position" # "Corridor Designer 4-Class Topographic Position" # nb_shape: "Circle" | "Annulus" # nb_units: "Cells" | "Meters" | "Kilometers" | "Feet" | "Miles" # tpi_type (on-the-fly): # "Raw (elevation units)" # "Neighborhood standard deviation" # "Percentile" # elev_units: "Meters" | "Feet" # slope_method: "Planar" | "Geodesic" # slope_units: "Degrees" | "Percent" # declare_tpi_type (existing mode, optional, warnings only): # "Raw (elevation units)" # "Neighborhood standard deviation" # "DEM-scale standard deviation" # "Percentile" # declare_slope_units (existing mode, optional, warnings only): # "Degrees" | "Percent"
# 1) compute TPI and slope on the fly from a DEM arcpy.jenness.SlopePositionClassification( tpi_source="Calculate TPI and Slope on-the-fly from DEM", in_raster="dem.tif", system="Weiss 6-Class Slope Position", out_raster="dem_SlopePos.tif", nb_shape="Circle", nb_outer=300, nb_inner=0, nb_units="Meters", tpi_type="Neighborhood standard deviation", elev_units="Meters", slope_method="Planar", slope_units="Degrees", save_tpi="dem_TPI.tif", save_slope="dem_Slope.tif")
# 2) classify existing TPI and slope rasters as-is (the rasters saved above; # the declare_* parameters are optional -- rasters made by these tools # carry their type in their metadata already) arcpy.jenness.SlopePositionClassification( tpi_source="Use Existing TPI and Slope Rasters", system="Weiss 6-Class Slope Position", out_raster="dem_SlopePos2.tif", in_tpi="dem_TPI.tif", in_slope="dem_Slope.tif", declare_tpi_type="Neighborhood standard deviation", declare_slope_units="Degrees")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Classify a DEM into slope-position classes (valley, slope, ridge, ...) from a TPI plus slope, using a saved classification system; TPI and slope computed internally, no Spatial Analyst.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Classifies a DEM into slope-position categories using the Topographic Position Index (elevation minus neighborhood mean; Weiss 2001) and slope, driven by a reusable, saved classification system (thresholds, names, colors). The neighborhood (circle or annulus, radius in cells or ground units) sets the analysis scale; the system's units may be raw TPI (absolute relief, usually best for wildlife questions) or standardized (relative to variability). TPI and slope are computed internally in numpy, and classification is a single vectorized pass (lowest class value wins on overlap) with no Spatial Analyst or Con. Output is an integer class raster with a Value/Class_Name attribute table and a color map. Bundled default systems: Weiss 6-class, Dickson and Beier 4-class, and the Corridor Designer 4-Class Topographic Position (canyon bottom / flat-gentle slope / steep slope / ridgetop; raw TPI, +/-12 m thresholds, 6-degree slope split, 200 m radius -- the corridor-analysis topographic factor from the CorridorDesigner tutorial).
dataIdInfo.idCredit: Tool by Jeff Jenness, Jenness Enterprises (http://www.jennessent.com). Method: Weiss, A. 2001. Topographic Position and Landforms Analysis. ESRI Int'l User Conf. poster; Guisan, A., et al. 1999. Plant Ecology 143:107-122 (https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1009841519580). Suggested citation: Jenness, J. (2026). Slope Position Classification. Jenness Enterprises Wildlife Tools for ArcGIS Pro. http://www.jennessent.com.
